name: alonzo-grounded-review
description: Orchestrate a high-assurance multi-agent review for this TypeScript, Bun, and OpenCode plugin repository. Use for repository-wide, security-sensitive, or correctness-critical review work.

# Alonzo Grounded Review

Adapt the `grounded-review` method from the local ai-toolkit to Alonzo's
sequential dispatcher. Ground the review in repository behavior first, run one
fresh lane at a time from a durable task queue, keep a genuinely independent
cold-read lane, have skeptics challenge findings and clearings, then resolve
disagreements before reporting.

## Grounding

Before reviewers start, the coordinator writes `.alonzo/review/grounding.md`
with:

- review scope and explicit out-of-scope items
- diff base and relevant commit range
- actual workflow, plugin, bridge, controller, editor, installer, and runtime
  behavior verified from source and tests
- an expected-behavior matrix for risky paths
- intended divergences and review-focus order

It also writes `.alonzo/review/review-plan.md` as a durable Markdown task table.
Use the columns `id`, `lane`, `status`, `depends_on`, `artifact`, `condition`,
and `notes`. Valid statuses are `pending`, `ready`, `completed`, and `skipped`.
Only one task may be `ready`; a task is ready only after every dependency is
terminal (`completed` or `skipped`). Mark a task completed only after its report
artifact contains an actual result. The coordinator returns exactly one
`work: <route-key>:` dispatch for the ready task, or `finalize:` when the whole
queue is terminal. Task IDs and route keys use the same underscore identifier,
so the runner can dispatch them deterministically. A phase router
first sends that dispatch to evidence review, validation, or
resolution/reporting; that phase's router then sends it to one fresh lane. The
lane returns to the coordinator to reconcile the plan again.

## Review Lanes

- `grounded_review` checks the implementation against grounding and records
  concrete unresolved watch-outs.
- `grounding_skeptic` treats the grounding-to-code match as wrong until traced.
- `unbiased_review` reads only code, commits, and tests. It must not read any
  `.alonzo/review/` artifact, design document, README, or product specification.
- `guided_watch_outs` runs only if earlier reports name a concrete unresolved
  target; otherwise the coordinator marks it skipped and records why.
- `unbiased_review_skeptic` re-verifies every unbiased finding and clearing
  against source and tests.
- `grounded_review_skeptic` challenges the grounded lane's findings and claimed
  clearings using the other completed lanes as evidence.
- `adjudication` resolves all reports against cited code and tests.
- `final_report` reports the adjudicated result and the terminal status of every
  lane.

Use this queue order and dependencies: grounded_review; grounding_skeptic after
grounded_review; unbiased_review after grounding_skeptic; guided_watch_outs
after unbiased_review; unbiased_review_skeptic after guided_watch_outs;
grounded_review_skeptic after unbiased_review_skeptic; adjudication after
grounded_review_skeptic; final_report after adjudication. Before starting a new
run, remove every prior lane report so an old artifact cannot satisfy a current
task.

Store reports in `.alonzo/review/` so later fresh child sessions can inspect
them without relying on a large handoff. The final report must distinguish
consensus, contested, single-source, cleared, and needs-follow-up findings.

## Mutation Testing

Use `mutation-tester` for one small reversible mutation at a time. It must save
a reversible patch, run the narrowest relevant test, restore the exact original
source, rerun the test, and verify no mutation residue remains. A surviving
mutation is a test gap, never a reason to retain the mutation.

# Alonzo Workflow Authoring

Create and edit `*.alonzo.yaml` workflows in the target project's `workflows/` directory. Do not write runtime data into `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/`; it is owned by Alonzo for traces and human-gate fallback files.

```yaml
alonzo: 1
name: my-workflow
start: first_step
nodes: {}
```

`alonzo`, `start`, and `nodes` are required. `name` and `layout` are optional. Do not use removed keys: top-level `state`, node `writes`, gate `writes`, or judge `{{input.*}}`/`{{output.*}}` state placeholders. The parser reports them as unknown keys.

Agent final text is the next node's handoff. Human, choice, and text gate responses are handoffs too. Use `payload: pass` on a router to preserve its incoming handoff and `payload: trigger` to clear it.

Use a judge when an agent result needs a pass/fail check:

```yaml
verify:
  judge:
    model: azure/deepseek-v4-flash
    prompt: Pass only when the candidate output is concise and complete.
```

The judge receives this authored prompt with the candidate output in a delimited context. Give every agent a clear handoff, ensure all targets exist, add defaults to LLM routers, and validate in the editor before running.

# Alonzo Workflow Operations

Use this skill to launch, inspect, or diagnose an Alonzo workflow run.

## Project Boundary

Alonzo has two directories:

- The **source checkout** contains the Bun launcher, editor, controller, docs,
  and adapter source. Run `bun run ui` from this directory.
- The **target project** contains the user's workflows and local `.opencode/`
  Alonzo installation. Start OpenCode or the UI launcher with this project as
  the target.

Do not assume Alonzo is globally installed. A target project needs the local
Alonzo installation before its own TUI can use `/alonzo`.

## Launch

For terminal use, open the OpenCode TUI from the installed target project:

```sh
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

Launch a workflow in OpenCode:

```text
/alonzo path/to/workflow.alonzo.yaml
```

Append optional user input after the path:

```text
/alonzo path/to/workflow.alonzo.yaml Review the latest authentication change.
```

Stop the active workflow for the calling session:

```text
/alonzo stop
```

## Editor Connectivity

From the Alonzo checkout, start the complete local stack for an installed project:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/project
```

The launcher starts OpenCode, the controller, and the editor. It waits for the bridge and opens a short-lived attached client only when required. Open the printed URL; the launcher target project is selected automatically and is the only project shown in the normal UI flow.

Default ports are OpenCode `4096`, controller `4097`, and editor `5173`. To run another stack, assign all three distinct ports:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/another-project \
  --opencode-port 4098 \
  --controller-port 4099 \
  --editor-port 5174
```

One launcher manages one project. The launcher fails before startup when a requested port is occupied. Press `Ctrl+C` in the launcher terminal to stop the local stack.

Do not start a separate OpenCode server for the editor workflow; the launcher
owns OpenCode, the controller, and the editor. If a port is occupied, stop the
previous launcher first. If its terminal is gone, identify the listener before
stopping it, or choose a distinct `--opencode-port`, `--controller-port`, and
`--editor-port` set.

## Inspect A Run

Check project-local runtime files:

- `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/trace/run-*.jsonl`
- `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/human/`

The trace is the source of truth for flow progression. Read it in order and identify the latest `transition`, `router_decision`, `human_gate`, `judge_*`, or `status_changed` entry.

## Common Problems

### The editor cannot connect

1. Confirm the `bun run ui` launcher is still running.
2. Confirm the controller and editor ports requested by the launcher are available.
3. Inspect the launcher terminal for an OpenCode or bridge startup error.
4. Stop the launcher with `Ctrl+C`, wait for it to exit, and start it again.
5. Refresh the editor; the launcher target project should select automatically.

### A previous run remains listed

Completed workflow sessions remain in OpenCode history, while the editor saves
its last selected workflow and session in browser site data. A fresh OpenCode
process replays only active in-memory runs; it does not scan old trace files.
Select another workflow or refresh the editor. If an unwanted historical session
is still selected, clear site data for the editor origin. Keep trace and human
files as diagnostics unless they are intentionally being discarded.

### A router does not advance

1. Confirm its prompt asks for a valid route key.
2. Confirm the returned route exists in `routes`.
3. Add a valid `default` target.

### A human gate does not resume

1. Check the editor for the gate dialog.
2. Inspect `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/human/` for the fallback request and response files.
3. Confirm the response satisfies the gate's configured constraints.

### A workflow halts on a provider error

Read the editor Logs tab and the terminal trace entry. Adjust the model or node prompt, then start a new run. Alonzo does not silently retry provider failures.

## Verify The Checkout

```sh

bun run test
bun run test:controller
bun run test:editor
bun run test:e2e
bun run test:repo
```

# Alonzo v0.1

Alonzo is a visual workflow editor for OpenCode. Design, run, and inspect YAML
workflow diagrams in the browser, with node-by-node messages, logs, routing,
human input, handoffs, and judge checks.

![Alonzo editor demo](docs/assets/alonzo-demo.gif)

**Workflows are executable agent instructions.** They can inspect or change the
selected project. Read node prompts, confirm the target project, and use a
disposable branch or test project for unfamiliar workflows.

## Start Here

1. [Getting Started](docs/GETTING-STARTED.md): install Alonzo and run your first workflow in the editor.
2. [Examples](docs/EXAMPLES.md): choose a safe first workflow.
3. [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md): resolve plugin, editor, model, and gate issues.

## What You Get

- YAML workflows in `*.alonzo.yaml` files
- Agent, router, and human-gate nodes
- Per-node OpenCode child sessions with `reuse` and `fresh` policies
- Optional user input delivered to the start node as workflow input
- Text handoffs between workflow nodes
- Optional judge retry checks for agent nodes
- JSONL traces and human-gate fallback files
- A browser editor for diagram authoring, execution, logs, and messages

## Repository Layout

- `core/`: workflow format, validator, runner, trace, and bridge protocol
- `adapter/`: OpenCode plugin, session orchestration, and editor bridge
- `controller/`: local controller for editor server discovery
- `editor/`: React workflow editor
- `workflows/`: ready-to-open workflows and editor-created project workflows
- `schema/`: JSON schema for `alonzo: 1` workflow files
- `skills/`: workflow authoring and operations instructions

## Requirements

- Bun
- OpenCode 1.17.19
- A target project where workflows may inspect or change files

Install repository dependencies from the root:

```sh
bun install
```

## Use The Editor

From the Alonzo checkout, start the local stack for an installed project:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/project
```

The launcher starts OpenCode, the controller, and the editor, then waits for the Alonzo bridge. Open the printed editor URL, normally `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.

The editor is automatically scoped to the launcher target project. Its project
picker lists editable workflows directly under that project's `workflows/`
directory. The editor creates new workflows in the same directory.

The installer adds `workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml`, a minimal one-node connectivity
check. The source checkout also includes `workflows/hey.alonzo.yaml` as an
optional interactive demo; copy it into a target project's `workflows/` directory
when wanted.

To open a different project, install Alonzo there and start another launcher with
that project's path. A browser cannot register an arbitrary local directory with
the running OpenCode server, so the editor does not provide a directory picker.

Default ports are OpenCode `4096`, controller `4097`, and editor `5173`. Override them when needed:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/project \
  --opencode-port 4098 \
  --controller-port 4099 \
  --editor-port 5174
```

One launcher manages one project. Multiple stacks can run only when every configured port is distinct. The launcher fails before startup when a requested port is occupied. Press `Ctrl+C` in the launcher terminal to stop the local stack.

## Use The TUI

For a terminal-only run, open the OpenCode TUI from the installed target project:

```sh
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

Then run a workflow with `/alonzo`:

```text
/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml
```

An optional prompt after the workflow path becomes the start node's workflow input:

```text
/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml Hello from the TUI.
```

Stop the current run with:

```text
/alonzo stop
```

## Local Runtime Data

Alonzo keeps project-local runtime data in `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/`:

- `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/trace/run-*.jsonl`: execution traces
- `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/human/`: human-gate fallback requests and responses

Bridge discovery is local controller state under `~/.config/opencode/alonzo/bridges/`. Both locations can contain project-sensitive data and are ignored by Git.

## Install Into Another Project

Use the cross-platform Bun installer to add Alonzo's project-local OpenCode files
to a target project:

```sh
bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts /path/to/target-project
```

The installer does not modify an existing target `opencode.json`. OpenCode
automatically discovers Alonzo from `.opencode/`. The generated plugin wrapper
imports this checkout's `adapter/src/plugin.ts`, so keep this checkout available
while the target project uses Alonzo.

If the launcher cannot start, a port is occupied, or the editor cannot connect,
see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) before retrying.

## Verify

Run these commands from the repository root:

```sh
bun run typecheck
bun run test
bun run test:controller
bun run test:editor
bun run test:e2e
bun run test:repo
```

# Alonzo Project Template

`scripts/install-opencode-template.ts` copies this template into a target project and creates the OpenCode configuration needed to load Alonzo.

The generated files are:

- `.opencode/commands/alonzo.md`
- `.opencode/plugins/alonzo.ts`
- `.opencode/package.json`
- `workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml`
- `.opencode/skills/alonzo-workflow-authoring/SKILL.md`
- `.opencode/skills/alonzo-workflow-ops/SKILL.md`

The generated plugin wrapper imports the Alonzo adapter from the source checkout used for installation. Keep that checkout available while the target project uses the template.

The installer leaves an existing target `opencode.json` untouched. OpenCode
automatically discovers the Alonzo plugin, command, and skills from `.opencode/`.

For the recommended visual workflow experience, run this from the Alonzo source
checkout:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project
```

Open the printed editor URL and start with `workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml`. For
terminal-only use, run `opencode` from the target project and enter
`/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml` in the TUI.

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 - 2026-08-04

First stable Alonzo release.

- Added a visual editor for creating, editing, running, and inspecting workflow diagrams.
- Added local editor launch, controller discovery, workflow persistence, run messages, logs, and human-gate handling.
- Added a `ping` starter workflow to the project installer.
- Added the `/alonzo` OpenCode TUI command for terminal-only workflow runs.
- Shipped workflow examples, validation, trace output, handoffs, routers, human gates, and judge checks.
- Standardized shipped workflow model fields on `azure/deepseek-v4-flash`.

# Architecture

Alonzo has four local components that work together without sending project paths through the browser.

## Core

`core/` owns workflow semantics:

- YAML parsing, validation, and serialization
- agent, router, and gate runner phases
- text handoffs and judge decisions
- node input overlays
- JSONL trace types and writing
- browser/bridge protocol types

The same format and validation code is used by the runtime and editor.

## OpenCode Adapter

`adapter/` is the OpenCode plugin layer. It loads workflows, creates a workflow parent session, creates child sessions for LLM nodes, dispatches runner effects, handles human gates, and streams trace and message data to the editor bridge.

Each run has one parent session. Agent and LLM-router nodes run in child sessions according to their `session_policy`. The final output of a node becomes workflow input for its successor unless a router uses `payload: trigger`.

## Controller

`controller/` is a loopback-only local service used by the editor. It discovers healthy Alonzo bridge instances and supplies the editor with the opaque server and project choices it needs. Browser code never receives a project filesystem path.

## Editor

`editor/` is the React and React Flow application. It requires explicit project selection before a workflow diagram can be opened or edited. It uses the bridge for project workflows, workflow runs, trace updates, messages, logs, and human-gate responses.

## Data Flow

1. OpenCode loads the plugin and starts a bridge instance.
2. The controller discovers that bridge instance.
3. The editor selects a server and project, then connects to the bridge.
4. The bridge loads and saves project workflow references such as `workflows/review.alonzo.yaml`.
5. A workflow run creates sessions, writes trace artifacts, and broadcasts editor updates.

## Local Data Boundaries

- Project workflow files: `workflows/`
- Project runtime data: `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/`
- Controller bridge discovery: `~/.config/opencode/alonzo/bridges/`

These locations are local operational data. Runtime data can contain project prompts, outputs, and local bridge authentication information.

# Editor Guide

The Alonzo editor is the recommended way to create, run, and inspect workflows.
Start it from the Alonzo source checkout for an installed target project:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project
```

Open the URL printed by the launcher, normally `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.
The editor is scoped to that target project and lists direct
`workflows/*.alonzo.yaml` files only.

## Workflow Selection

Choose a workflow from the `Workflow` menu or use `New` to create a local
workflow. Local workflows are stored under the target project's `workflows/`
directory. Global workflows, when configured in the controller, appear with a
`Global` label; running one materializes a project-local copy for execution.

The initial installer workflow is `ping`. It is a safe connectivity check. Copy
other examples from this checkout into the target project's `workflows/`
directory before selecting them.

## Edit Mode

Use `Mode` > `Edit` to change a workflow.

- Select a node to open its settings in the side panel.
- Use `Add` to click-add an agent, router, or gate near the workflow start node.
- Drag an `Add` button onto the canvas to choose a position directly.
- Drag between node handles to create a connection. Select an edge to adjust or
  remove its control point.
- Drag nodes to save their canvas positions.
- Use `Undo` and `Redo` for document changes.
- Use `Save` to write the selected workflow. The button is pale when the current
  document matches the last saved version and blue when there are unsaved edits.

Each selected node also has common controls:

- **Name**: a unique identifier beginning with a letter; it may contain letters,
  numbers, hyphens, and underscores.
- **Rotate**: changes only the canvas presentation.
- **Set start**: makes the node the workflow entry point.
- **Delete**: removes the node and its attached edges.

Connections define `next` for agent and gate nodes, and route targets for router
nodes. The canvas layout is editor metadata; it does not change runtime logic.

## View Mode

Use `Mode` > `View` to run and inspect the selected workflow.

1. Enter optional input in the run panel. It becomes the start node's workflow
   input.
2. Select `Run`.
3. Use `Stop` to cancel the active run.
4. Open the side-panel `Messages` and `Logs` tabs to inspect the execution.

Selecting a node in View mode shows its current status, resolved configuration,
last route or corrective message, and its five most recent messages. Node colors
and edges also show progress: running, completed, correcting, error, and visited
paths are visually distinct.

## Agent Nodes

Agent nodes ask an OpenCode agent to perform work. Their settings are:

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **agent** | OpenCode agent to invoke. The picker reflects agents available from the connected server. |
| **model** | Optional `provider/model` override. Leave it blank to use the selected agent's configured model. |
| **session_policy** | `reuse` keeps the node's child session for later visits; `fresh` creates a new child session each time. |
| **prompt** | The instruction for this node. The runtime also supplies workflow input and relevant execution context. |
| **Judge (verify)** | Optional pass/fail review of the agent output. Enable it to set the judge model and criteria prompt. Alonzo supplies the candidate output to the judge. The View panel shows the latest verdict when available. |

Connect the outgoing edge to choose the next node. A node with no outgoing edge
is terminal.

## Router Nodes

Routers choose a route key and send execution to that route's target.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **mode** | `llm` asks the configured agent/model to choose a route. `human` presents route choices to the user and does not make an LLM call. |
| **agent** and **model** | Available only for `llm` routers. A blank model uses the agent default. |
| **payload** | `pass` forwards the incoming handoff to the selected next node. `trigger` clears that handoff and only triggers the selected node. |
| **prompt** | The routing instruction or the question shown for a human router. |
| **routes** | Rows of route key, target node, and optional description. Route keys label the canvas branches; descriptions explain choices on router cards and in human choices. |
| **default** | LLM routers only. Target used after an undecidable LLM route. Human routers do not expose a selectable default; connected routes are presented as choices. |

Add route rows with `Add route`. Blank or duplicate keys are ignored until fixed.
Make route targets match existing node names. Use the warnings bar to resolve any
invalid or disconnected routes before running.

## Gate Nodes

Gate nodes pause the workflow for user input. Their settings are:

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **gate kind** | `human`, `choice`, or `text`. Changing kind resets that gate's kind-specific settings. |
| **prompt** | The question or instruction shown to the user. |
| **choice options** | For a choice gate, one option per line. Empty lines are ignored. |
| **min length** / **max length** | For a text gate, the accepted response-size bounds. |

Use the outgoing edge to define the node that receives the gate response as its
workflow input. A gate response can be submitted in the editor or through the
TUI. If no browser client owns the request, Alonzo writes a file fallback under
`.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/human/`.

## Saving And Errors

The editor validates the document before a local save or run. The warnings bar
identifies malformed node names, missing targets, invalid route definitions,
unreachable nodes, and other format problems. Provider failures stop the active
workflow; inspect `Logs`, adjust the node model or prompt, and explicitly run
again.

For the YAML-level format, validation rules, and semantics not exposed in the
editor, see [Workflow Format](FORMAT.md). For startup, port, connection, and
session-history recovery, see [Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md).

Copy an example from this checkout into the target project's `workflows/`

# Workflow Format

Alonzo workflows are `*.alonzo.yaml` files. The editor and runtime share the parser, serializer, and validator from `@alonzo/core`.

```yaml
alonzo: 1
name: summarize-change
start: summarize
nodes:
  summarize:
    agent: general
    prompt: Summarize the requested change and return a concise handoff.
```

`alonzo`, `start`, and `nodes` are required. `$schema`, `name`, and `layout` are optional. Unknown keys are errors, including removed legacy keys `state`, node `writes`, and gate `writes`.

## Handoffs

An agent's final text is the handoff delivered to the next agent. Human, choice, and text gate responses also become the next handoff. An optional run prompt is the start node's handoff.

## Nodes

Agent nodes support `agent`, `model`, `session_policy`, `prompt`, `verify`, and `next`. Routers select a target from `routes`; use `payload: pass` to preserve an incoming handoff or `payload: trigger` to clear it. Human-mode routers present route choices without an LLM call.

```yaml
review:
  agent: general
  prompt: Review the implementation and return concise findings.
  verify:
    judge:
      prompt: Pass only when the findings are actionable and complete.
  next: route_review
```

Judges receive the authored prompt and the candidate node output in a clearly delimited context. They return pass/fail verdicts; failed verdicts retain the existing retry behavior.

```yaml
ask_human:
  kind: gate
  prompt: Provide the missing release context.
  gate:
    kind: text
    minLength: 1
    maxLength: 2000
  next: review
```

`layout` is editor metadata and does not change runtime behavior. Validation checks node targets, required fields, router consistency, reachability, and cycles.

# Getting Started

Alonzo has two directories: the **source checkout**, where you run Bun commands,
and a **target project**, whose files workflows can inspect or modify.

## Before You Run

Workflows are executable agent instructions, not passive YAML. Read node prompts,
confirm the selected target project, and use a disposable branch or test project
for unfamiliar workflows.

## Prerequisites

Install Bun and OpenCode, then check them:

```sh
bun --version
opencode --version
```

Alonzo v0.1 is tested with OpenCode `1.17.19`.

## Install

From the Alonzo source checkout:

```sh
bun install
bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts /path/to/target-project
```

The installer creates a target-project OpenCode integration: the `/alonzo`
command, plugin wrapper, skills, and the `ping` workflow. It leaves
an existing `opencode.json` untouched because OpenCode automatically discovers
Alonzo from the target project's `.opencode/` directory. The generated wrapper
imports this source checkout by path, so do not move the checkout while the
target project uses Alonzo.

## Five-Minute Editor Run

1. From the source checkout, start the local editor stack:

   ```sh
   bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project
   ```

2. Open the printed URL, normally `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.
3. Select `ping` to verify provider connectivity. It is installed under the
   target project's `workflows/` directory.
4. In View mode, run the workflow and inspect Messages and Logs. Switch to Edit
   mode to change the diagram and save it.

The launcher starts OpenCode, the controller, and the editor. It scopes the
editor to the target project, so only that project's direct
`workflows/*.alonzo.yaml` files can be opened or created.

Keep the launcher terminal open while using the editor. Press `Ctrl+C` there to
stop the entire local stack. If startup fails, do not start OpenCode separately;
use the recovery steps in [Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md).

## Run From The TUI

For a terminal-only workflow run, start OpenCode in the installed target project:

```sh
cd /path/to/target-project
opencode
```

Then enter `/alonzo` in the TUI:

```text
/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml
```

Append input after the path when needed, for example:

```text
/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml Hello from the TUI.
```

Use `/alonzo stop` to stop the active workflow in that TUI session.

# Maintenance Notes

Internal follow-up record. This file tracks concrete maintenance work; it is
not part of the user-facing workflow guide.

## UI Launcher And Project Scope

`bun run ui -- --project <path>` must run from the Alonzo source checkout.
The command starts code from this repository: the controller, Vite editor, and
an OpenCode server rooted in the selected project.

The plugin is not globally installed. A target project receives a local Alonzo
wrapper through `bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts <target-project>`.
The source checkout itself is also accepted by the launcher because its root
`opencode.json` imports `adapter/src/plugin.ts` directly.

Once an Alonzo bridge is running, the browser can list and select every project
known to that OpenCode server. That does not mean Alonzo has been installed
into each listed project. It means the single running plugin instance can use
OpenCode's project-scoped API client for a selected project. TUI use from a
different project still requires that project to have the local installation.

## Live Example Acceptance

Use isolated installed target projects for workflow acceptance. A source-checkout
custom command can be expanded by OpenCode as an ordinary prompt when the plugin
hook is not active; it is not valid evidence of workflow execution.

The live harness uses `opencode run --attach <server> --command alonzo` and the
Alonzo bridge to inspect workflow node messages, terminal status, and gates.
OpenCode persists sessions and messages in its local database and exposes them
through its server session/message API.

Gate responses sent over the bridge must include both `requestID` and
`sessionID`; missing session identity is rejected to prevent a client from
answering another workflow's gate. File-based gate responses remain the fallback
when no bridge client owns a gate.

## Whole-Repository Review Workflow

Establish a review skill for this TypeScript/Bun/OpenCode plugin repository.

The existing C++-oriented multi-agent review process should be adapted before
use. The review should cover:

- TypeScript and Bun runtime behavior
- OpenCode plugin, command, skill, config, and SDK lifecycle contracts
- HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, and process lifecycle handling
- browser/client trust boundaries and filesystem-path isolation
- workflow format and runner state-machine invariants
- installer, template, documentation, and acceptance-path correctness
- test gaps across core, adapter, controller, editor, and live acceptance

Before creating the review skill, inventory the available OpenCode agents and
the repository's existing skills. Use the resulting review process against the
full repository, not only the workflow database.

# Running Alonzo

Alonzo runs inside an OpenCode server. OpenCode automatically loads the project
plugin and `/alonzo` command from `.opencode/`, then the plugin starts a local
bridge for the editor.

## Start The Editor

The editor is the recommended way to author, run, and inspect workflows. From
the Alonzo checkout, start the complete local editor stack for an installed
target project:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project
```

The launcher starts OpenCode, the controller, and the Vite editor. It prints the
browser URL, normally `http://127.0.0.1:5173`, and scopes the editor to the
launcher target project. Then:

1. Create a workflow or open one from `workflows/`.
2. Use View mode to run it and inspect messages, logs, and human gates.
3. Use Edit mode to change the diagram and save it.

The installer adds `workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml` as a safe starting point. The
editor lists and edits direct `workflows/*.alonzo.yaml` files only; copy other
repository examples, including the interactive `hey` demo, into the target
project's `workflows/` directory before opening them.

See the [Editor Guide](EDITOR.md) for editing, running, node settings, and
execution inspection.

Keep the launcher terminal open while using the editor. Press `Ctrl+C` there to
stop the complete local stack. Do not start a separate OpenCode server for this
editor workflow; the launcher owns it.

## Run From The TUI

For a terminal-only run, open the OpenCode TUI from the installed target project:

```sh
cd /path/to/target-project
opencode
```

Run a workflow with:

```text
/alonzo path/to/workflow.alonzo.yaml
```

Append optional user input after the path:

```text
/alonzo path/to/workflow.alonzo.yaml Review the latest authentication change.
```

The workflow prompt configured on the start agent remains its task. The user input is injected as the start node's `Workflow input`, just as downstream nodes receive upstream workflow input.

Stop the active workflow in the calling session:

```text
/alonzo stop
```

Default ports are OpenCode `4096`, controller `4097`, and editor `5173`. To run another stack, assign all three different ports:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/another-project \
  --opencode-port 4098 \
  --controller-port 4099 \
  --editor-port 5174
```

One launcher manages one project. The launcher fails before startup when any requested port is already occupied. Press `Ctrl+C` in the launcher terminal to stop the child processes.

For startup, port, bridge, and stale-run recovery, see
[Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md).

## Runtime Data

Project-local runtime data is written to `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/`:

- `trace/run-*.jsonl`: ordered transitions, routing, gates, and terminal status
- `human/`: file-based human-gate fallback requests and responses

The controller stores bridge discovery records in `~/.config/opencode/alonzo/bridges/`. Do not commit or share either location without reviewing it for project content and local authentication tokens.

## Failure Handling

When OpenCode or a provider rejects a prompt, Alonzo halts the workflow and records a safe error in the trace and editor Logs tab. It does not automatically retry with another model or alter your prompt. Update the node configuration, then explicitly start another run.

## Install Template

The cross-platform project template installer wires another project to this source checkout:

```sh
bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts /path/to/target-project
```

It creates the target project's `.opencode/` plugin, command, skills, and starter
workflows without modifying an existing `opencode.json`. The wrapper imports
`adapter/src/plugin.ts` from the source checkout used during installation, so
keep that checkout available while using the target project.

# Troubleshooting

The editor launcher is the normal browser workflow:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project
```

Run it from the Alonzo source checkout, not from the target project. Keep that
terminal open while using the editor. It starts and stops OpenCode, the
controller, and the editor together.

## Start With These Checks

1. Confirm the source checkout has its dependencies:

   ```sh
   bun install
   ```

2. Confirm the target path exists and Alonzo is installed there:

   ```sh
   bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts /path/to/target-project
   ```

   The installer creates `.opencode/plugins/alonzo.ts`, the `/alonzo` command,
   skills, and starter workflows. It leaves any existing `opencode.json`
   untouched.

3. Confirm OpenCode is available:

   ```sh
   opencode --version
   ```

4. Start the editor stack once. Do not separately start OpenCode for the same
   project and ports.

## The Launcher Says Alonzo Is Not Installed

The target project does not contain the local plugin wrapper, or the launcher
was pointed at the wrong directory. Run the installer from the source checkout:

```sh
bun scripts/install-opencode-template.ts /path/to/target-project
```

If the target already has `opencode.json`, leave it in place. The installer adds
Alonzo beneath `.opencode/` without modifying the existing configuration.

## OpenCode Does Not Start In The Target Project

Read the launcher terminal from the first error. Common causes are:

- `opencode` is not on `PATH`: install OpenCode or set `OPENCODE_BIN` to its
  executable path before starting the launcher.
- The target project's `opencode.json` is invalid: run `opencode` directly from
  that project to see the configuration error, fix it, then stop that TUI and
  retry the launcher.
- The source checkout was moved after installation: rerun the installer so the
  generated `.opencode/plugins/alonzo.ts` wrapper points at the current checkout.
- Another OpenCode process already owns the configured port: stop it or use a
  different three-port set as described below.

## A Port Is Already In Use

The launcher reserves three different loopback ports before starting: OpenCode
`4096`, controller `4097`, and editor `5173`. First stop the previous launcher
with `Ctrl+C` in its terminal. If that terminal is gone, identify the listener
before killing it.

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen -LocalPort 4096,4097,5173 |
  Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess
Get-Process -Id <pid>
Stop-Process -Id <pid>
```

On macOS or Linux:

```sh
lsof -nP -iTCP:4096 -sTCP:LISTEN
lsof -nP -iTCP:4097 -sTCP:LISTEN
lsof -nP -iTCP:5173 -sTCP:LISTEN
kill <pid>
```

Verify the process is an old OpenCode, controller, or Vite instance before
stopping it. If it belongs to another application, leave it running and select
three unused ports instead:

```sh
bun run ui -- --project /path/to/target-project \
  --opencode-port 4098 \
  --controller-port 4099 \
  --editor-port 5174
```

All three port values must be different.

## The Editor Cannot Connect Or Shows No Server

1. Keep the launcher terminal open and check it reached `Alonzo editor is ready`.
2. Open the exact URL printed by the launcher. It is usually
   `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.
3. Stop the launcher with `Ctrl+C`, wait for it to exit, then start it again.
4. If the launcher reports that the bridge did not initialize, check the
   OpenCode startup error above. A fresh launcher restart is safer than manually
   starting only one of its child processes.

## The Editor Shows No Workflows

The editor lists only direct `workflows/*.alonzo.yaml` files in its target
project. The installer adds `ping.alonzo.yaml`. Copy other examples, including
`hey.alonzo.yaml`, from this checkout into the target project's `workflows/` directory;
nested files and source-checkout examples are not listed automatically.

## A Previous Run Is Still Listed

OpenCode keeps completed workflow parent sessions in its local session history,
and the editor remembers the last selected workflow and session in browser site
data. This can make a previous run remain selectable after a launcher restart.

Only active in-memory workflow runs replay trace entries after a browser
reconnect. Alonzo does not scan `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/trace/` on startup, so
old trace files are diagnostics, not replay input.

To return to a fresh editor view, select another workflow or refresh the page.
If the browser continues to select an unwanted historical session, clear site
data for the editor origin, normally `http://127.0.0.1:5173`, then reopen the
editor. This clears saved editor selection and prompts; it does not delete
workflows, OpenCode session history, or runtime diagnostics.

Keep `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/trace/` and `human/` until you have reviewed any
failure or gate evidence. Delete individual runtime artifacts only when you
intentionally want to discard those diagnostics.

## `/alonzo` Is Normal Text In The TUI

The TUI command is separate from the editor launcher. Confirm the target project
has the generated `.opencode/` integration, then start the TUI from that target
project:

```sh
cd /path/to/target-project
opencode
```

Enter `/alonzo workflows/ping.alonzo.yaml` in that TUI. If it is still treated as
normal text, inspect the project's OpenCode configuration and plugin wrapper.

## A Model Fails

Check that the selected model is available in the target project's OpenCode
providers, or update the affected node configuration. Start a new run after the
change; Alonzo does not silently switch models.

## A Workflow Waits At A Gate

Submit the requested response in the editor or TUI. File fallback requests and
responses are under `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/human/` in the target project.

## A Workflow Halts

Inspect the editor Logs tab and traces under `.opencode/alonzo/.alonzo/trace/`.
Fix the node configuration or prompt and start a new run. Provider errors halt
the workflow rather than changing the model or rewriting the workflow.

## Before Sharing Diagnostics

Traces, handoffs, messages, gate files, and bridge records can contain project
content or local authentication information. Review them before sharing.
